analysis.one_liner: Exempts all voluntary private economic agreements from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have freed private agreements from antitrust enforcement, drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have removed the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, and the FTC's competition authority from any agreement between individuals or groups. In practice, that means companies could agree to fix prices, divide up markets, or coordinate wages without breaking the law, and large mergers and monopolies would face far less scrutiny. It was introduced in the Senate's final days, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and industries that want to coordinate prices, divide customers, or suppress competition would gain the most, since the core antitrust laws would no longer apply to their agreements. Dominant firms would also face weaker legal tools against monopolistic behavior, and employers coordinating on wages would be shielded from antitrust challenge.

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts any 'voluntary economic coordination, cooperation, agreement, or other association' from the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, and section 5 of the FTC Act, the three pillars of federal antitrust enforcement [S3].

Under the CRS summary, antitrust and unfair-competition laws would not apply to agreements between individuals or groups of individuals, removing legal barriers to collusion that currently expose price-fixing to lawsuits and FTC action [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay higher prices where firms fix them, workers would face less competition for their labor where employers coordinate, and small businesses would compete against larger rivals freed from antitrust limits. The public would bear these costs with no compensation elsewhere in the bill.

drawbacks.text: Exempting agreements from the Sherman Act would remove the main legal check on price-fixing and market allocation, the practices antitrust law has prohibited for more than a century, likely leading to higher prices for consumers [S3].

Because 'any group of individuals' is exempted, employers could coordinate on wages and working conditions with less fear of antitrust challenge, weakening workers' bargaining position, and dominant firms would face fewer limits on acquisitions and exclusionary conduct [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers its stated benefit — freedom from antitrust liability for voluntary contracts — but its practical effect would be to legalize the collusion antitrust law exists to stop. The costs fall broadly on consumers and workers while the gains accrue to firms with market power, and the bill received no cosponsors, suggesting little appetite even among its sponsor's colleagues.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's last two weeks and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on December 17, 2020, in the Senate's final session days [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and workers came out ahead, since the antitrust protections that restrain price-fixing and employer coordination remain in force. Firms seeking freedom to collude or merge freely lost the chance, having gained no traction for the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and workers kept antitrust protections

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan shape of the bill's support and opposition is unknown.

industries.note: Exempting private agreements from the Sherman Act, Clayton Act, and FTC Act would free firms to fix prices, divide markets, and consolidate without antitrust liability, which is exactly the conduct those laws prohibit [S3]. The gains come at consumers' expense through higher prices and reduced competition.

industries.industry: Employers coordinating on wages and labor
industries.note: Employer agreements on wages or no-poach arrangements are currently exposed to antitrust challenge; exempting agreements among 'any group of individuals' would shield that coordination [S3]. This weakens workers' leverage without providing any offsetting benefit to them.

Antitrust law is a key tool small firms use against exclusionary conduct by dominant rivals; with the Clayton Act and FTC authority not applying to private agreements, smaller competitors would face weaker recourse [S3].
